c.tagline: The Marianas' laid-back main island — turquoise dive sites, WWII history, and endless summer.

taxi.fareNote: No ride-hailing apps operate on Saipan. Getting around means metered or flat-rate taxis (airport to Garapan runs about $20-30, though many hotels offer a cheaper flat shuttle) or — by far the most practical option — a rental car.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number, as on the US mainland; the Commonwealth Health Center in Garapan is the island's main hospital.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

hood_landmark.San Antonio: San Antonio Saipan Coral Ocean Resort

avoid.reason: Car break-ins happen at quiet beach parks and viewpoints, so leave nothing in rental cars, and watch for stray dogs on back roads.

hood_desc: The island's tourist heart on the west coast: the main strip of hotels, restaurants, bars, and duty-free shops backing onto Micro Beach and American Memorial Park — the base for most visitors.
The adjoining administrative and local-life districts wrapped around Saipan's calm western lagoon, with the courts, sugar-dock beaches, and everyday shops; quieter and more residential than Garapan.
A southern residential village near the airport and the reef-fringed south coast, home to Coral Ocean Resort and its golf course; low-key and convenient for arrivals.
The breezy hillside seat of the CNMI government above Garapan, with Japanese-era ruins and cooler air; residential and green, a quiet base with a car.
The wild northern tip of the island, uninhabited apart from its sights: Banzai Cliff, the Last Command Post, Bird Island lookout, and the world-famous Grotto dive site.

water.note: Island tap water is often brackish and not reliably potable; drink bottled water.

transit.hours: Public transport is minimal; a limited shuttle serves some routes during the day. Most visitors rely on rental cars or taxis.
transit.note: Saipan has no real public transit system beyond a limited shuttle plus hotel and tour shuttles. A rental car is the standard way to get around; taxis are available but pricey.
transit.pay: Taxis are paid in cash or by card in US dollars; there is no transit-card system. Rental cars are widely available at the airport and in Garapan.

ferry: Managaha Island transfer boats from Garapan

transit.m: Hotel shuttle to Garapan (flat rate, often ~$10 per person)

tip.r: US-style tipping: ~15-20% at restaurants and for taxis and guides.

landmarks: Managaha Island
A tiny islet ringed by powder-white sand in Saipan's lagoon, the archipelago's favourite day trip for snorkelling, parasailing and postcard views.
The Grotto
A collapsed limestone cavern where a stairway descends to a luminous blue pool, rated among the world's most spectacular cavern dive sites.
Banzai Cliff
A windswept northern promontory with memorials to the hundreds who leapt into the sea in 1944, now a solemn place of pilgrimage and remembrance.
Suicide Cliff
The 249-metre precipice above Marpi where memorial gardens and peace monuments overlook the site of the battle's tragic final days.
Last Command Post
The cliffside bunker where Japanese forces made their final stand in 1944, its rusting guns and tanks framed by dramatic Marpi cliffs.
Bird Island Lookout
A postcard viewpoint over a wildlife-sanctuary islet rising from turquoise reef flats on Saipan's rugged northeastern coast.
American Memorial Park
A U.S. national park on the Garapan waterfront honouring the Marianas campaign with museums, flag circle, beaches and shady walking trails.
Mount Tapochau
Saipan's 474-metre summit at the island's centre, crowned by a Christ statue and offering 360-degree views over lagoon, reef and Philippine Sea.
Micro Beach
Garapan's calm, sunset-facing strand of white sand and shallow turquoise water, widely considered the most beautiful beach on Saipan proper.
Forbidden Island
A wild, ruggedly beautiful islet and marine sanctuary reached by a steep hike, hiding tidal pools and coves along Saipan's untamed east coast.

train.note: There is no railway in the Northern Marianas. Arrive by air into Saipan International Airport, with flights from Guam, Japan, Korea and the Philippines. There is no rail anywhere in Micronesia.

bus.note: No international coaches - Saipan is an island. Public transport is minimal: a limited shuttle service runs along the Garapan hotel strip and to the shopping areas, and most visitors hire a car. Taxis are available but not plentiful. There is no terminal.

intl.op: Tinian Express / local ferry operators — tickets at the Saipan dock

ferry.note: There is no scheduled international ferry - travel to Guam and beyond is by air. The Tinian crossing has operated intermittently over the years and is the only regular boat service, taking about an hour from the Saipan seaport; confirm it is running before relying on it. Dive and snorkel boats to Managaha island are day excursions.

full.name: Tinian
full.blurb: A short ferry or flight reaches an island where the atomic bomb loading pits and a former World War Two airfield remain preserved.

full.name: Rota
full.blurb: A short flight reaches a quieter island known for limestone caves, a bird sanctuary, and a much smaller population than Saipan.
